messages.subject: meanstructure/intercept in pathmodel
parts:
Dear list,

I am using lavaan to model relatively simple correlations between three variables. x, y1, y2.
Furthermore, I want to force the correlations y1 ~ x and y2 ~ x through the origin [similar to a linear model without intercept lm(y1 ~ x - 1)].
Then the model structure would look like this:

mod1 <-
"##### regressions
y1 + y2 ~ x
##### variances and covariances
y1 ~~ y1
y2 ~~ y2
y1 ~~ y2
##### regression forced through origin (without intercept)
y1 + y2 ~ 0*1"

mod1 <- sem(mod1_ph, data = pic_data_scaled, fixed.x=FALSE)

When I read the tutorials I wondered, however, how the modelfit is affected if I also fix the mean of the
exogenous variable (x) to zero. Then the model would look like this:

mod2_ph <-
"##### regressions
y1 + y2 ~ x
##### variances and covariances
y1 ~~ y1
y2 ~~ y2
y1 ~~ y2
##### regression forced through origin,
# mean of x set to zero
y1 + y2 + x ~ 0*1"

mod2 <- sem(mod2_ph, data = pic_data_scaled, fixed.x=TRUE)

Does this affect the model estimates? and in which way?

I hope anyone can help me.

Thanks a lot,

Jörg

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: meanstructure/intercept in pathmodel
parts:
Jorg--
     Yes, forcing the mean of X to 0 will affect the results, and not in a good way.  The strength of the effect depends on how far away from 0 the mean of X really is.  The farther away, the more the variance of X will be inflated, tending to weaken the calculated correlation between X and Y, thus weakening the calculated regression slope.
     You can compute the regression slope as:

B = covariance (Y,X) / variance (X)

and compute the terms on the right as:

Covariance (Y,X) = SUM [(Y - mean(Y))(X - mean(X))] / n
Variance (X) = SUM [(X - mean(X)) squared] / n

summed across all X,Y pairs

Replacing the mean of X with 0 gets you:

Covariance (Y,X) = SUM [(Y - mean(Y))(X)] / n
Variance (X) = SUM [(X) squared] / n

To see the effect, replace X with:

X = X - mean(X) + (mean(X)

in the equations above.  In the variance(X) equation, things get squared, and so replacing the actual mean of X with 0 rapidly inflates the variance, while also inflating the covariance, but not by so much.  So the denominator of the slope equation increases much more rapidly than the numerator, and the computed slope is attenuated.
--Ed Rigdon
